stimulus.text:
“He has kept among us, in times of peace, Standing Armies without the Consent of our legislatures. … He has cut off our Trade with all parts of the world. … He has plundered our seas, ravaged our Coasts, burnt our towns, and destroyed the lives of our people.”
—Declaration of Independence, July 4, 1776 (abridged)

books.section: Topic 3.5 The American Revolution, A. The War for Independence

stem: Beyond justifying independence to Americans, the Declaration's list of the king's abuses was most directly aimed at

options.text: Ordering colonial militias to attack British forts
options.misconception: The Declaration justifies independence; it gives no orders to militias and names no forts to attack.

options.text: Repealing the taxes Parliament had imposed on the colonies
options.misconception: A declaration cannot repeal British taxes; only Parliament could do that, and it did not.

options.text: Settling the boundaries of the new states
options.misconception: The Declaration draws no boundaries; the Treaty of Paris in 1783 set the nation's borders.

options.text: Persuading foreign powers, especially France, that the cause was just

rationales.D: A published list of a king's crimes was addressed to the world: it told foreign courts that the Americans were a people with a just cause worth aiding.
rationales.A: The Declaration is a political argument, not a military order; it commands no attack on any fort.
rationales.B: Declaring independence does not repeal a tax; the taxes stayed until Britain lost the war.
rationales.C: Boundaries were settled by the Treaty of Paris in 1783, not by the Declaration in 1776.
rationales.general:
1. Ask who else would read it. The Declaration was printed and sent abroad, not kept in Congress.
2. Ask what a foreign court needs. A king's crimes, listed in order, give France a reason to treat rebels as a lawful nation.
3. Check the timing. France allied with the United States in 1778, after Saratoga showed the cause could win.
Remember: a document written for the world is doing diplomacy, not just argument — ask whose help it hopes to win. Background: France formally allied with the United States in 1778.
